Hades. The Olympian god of the underworld, death, and the dead in Greek and Roman mythology, ruling over the souls of the deceased from his shadowy subterranean palace. One of the three paramount gods alongside Zeus and Poseidon, Hades is often portrayed as less capricious and more austere than his brothers, less interested in human affairs than in maintaining the boundaries between the living and the dead. He is wealthy in precious minerals and is associated with fertility as well as death through his abduction of Persephone.

Hades is one of the three cosmic rulers. Zeus governs the sky, Poseidon the sea, and Hades the underworld, each supreme in their realm, though Zeus holds ultimate authority. He rules over all the dead without exception. Souls of the deceased descend to his domain regardless of their virtue or vice, making him the most impartial of gods. Death, for him, is no respecter of persons. He married Persephone, daughter of Demeter, whom he abducted into the underworld. The myth explains the seasons through their marriage: Persephone spends half the year with Hades, causing Demeter's grief and winter's dormancy.

Hades is guarded by Cerberus, a three-headed dog, who prevents the living from entering and the dead from leaving. Cerberus is the most famous gatekeeper in mythology and embodies Hades' function as boundary-keeper. The name Hades refers both to the god and the place, the underworld itself. Roman equivalents include Pluto and Dis, used interchangeably in later literature. He is generally portrayed as stern, grim, and not easily moved by prayer. Unlike Zeus and other gods, he does not favor mortals with gifts or alter his judgments. His realm is governed by inexorable law. He is also associated with wealth and precious metals mined from the earth, giving him a darker economic aspect. In some fertility cults, he is a chthonic, or earth-dwelling, god of grain and agricultural bounty beneath the surface, linking him to cycles of renewal even as he presides over death.
